draft.title: Molar mass and moles
card: Molar mass (M) is the mass of one mole of a substance. Its unit is g/mol.
For an element, the molar mass in g/mol has the same number as its relative atomic mass on the periodic table. Carbon is about 12.01 g/mol.
For a compound, add the molar masses of all the atoms in its formula. Water, H2O, is 2 × 1.008 + 16.00 = 18.02 g/mol.
Moles, mass and molar mass are linked by n = m/M. Here n is moles (mol) and m is mass in grams (g). Rearranged, m = n × M.
draft.remember: Divide the mass in grams by the molar mass to get moles.

a.q: A sample of water, H2O, has a mass of 36.04 g. The molar mass of water is 18.02 g/mol. How many moles of water are in the sample?
a.why: n = m/M = 36.04 ÷ 18.02 = 2.000 mol. Dividing the other way, 18.02 ÷ 36.04, gives 0.5000 mol, which turns the formula upside down.
a.clue: Mass goes on top and molar mass goes on the bottom.

b.q: Priya has 0.250 mol of sodium chloride, NaCl. Na is 22.99 g/mol and Cl is 35.45 g/mol. What mass of NaCl does she have?
b.why: M of NaCl = 22.99 + 35.45 = 58.44 g/mol. m = n × M = 0.250 × 58.44 = 14.6 g. Dividing 0.250 by 58.44 would give 0.00428, which is the wrong way round for finding mass.
b.clue: Find the molar mass first, then multiply by the moles.

problems.detail: "For an element, the molar mass ... has the same number as its relative atomic mass" does not hold for elements that exist as molecules. O2 is 32.00 g/mol, not 16.00. Students may divide by 16.00 for oxygen gas. It would help to say this applies to the element's atoms, or to note diatomic elements.

check.summary: Both questions and explanations are correct: 2.000 mol and 14.6 g. One small risk: the card's line on elements could lead students to use the atomic mass for diatomic elements like O2.
